title: Explain One Idea with an Analogy and Its Limit
subtitle: Create Analogies
description: Compare an unfamiliar idea with something familiar, state the matching point, name where the comparison stops and ask the listener to restate the idea.

lifeOsSource.hack: Explain one unfamiliar idea by comparing it with something the listener already knows, then state the exact point of comparison and where the analogy stops.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: Write the idea you need to explain. Choose a familiar comparison, map only the important relationship, add one boundary sentence and ask the listener to restate the original idea. Revise the analogy if the restatement keeps the wrong detail.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: Could the listener restate the intended idea, and which part of the analogy clarified or distorted it?

faq.question: How do I know whether an analogy is useful?
faq.answer: Ask the listener to explain the original idea in their own words. A memorable comparison is not useful if it preserves the wrong relationship.

faq.question: What if the listener takes the analogy literally?
faq.answer: State the boundary directly: explain which part matches and which part does not. Replace the analogy when the boundary needs more explanation than the idea itself.
faq.answerHtml: State the boundary directly: explain which part matches and which part does not. Replace the analogy when the boundary needs more explanation than the idea itself.

faq.question: Should I use the same analogy for every audience?
faq.answer: No. Choose a familiar source for the specific listener and avoid comparisons that carry distracting, loaded or misleading associations.

intro.html: An analogy can make a structure easier to see, but it also imports assumptions from the familiar example. The practice is not merely to invent a vivid comparison. It is to map one useful relationship, expose the limit and check what the listener understood.

sections.title: 1. Define the idea you need to explain
sections.html: Write one sentence describing the target idea without an analogy. This gives you something to compare the listener's later restatement against.

sections.title: 2. Choose a familiar source
sections.html: Pick an object, activity or system the listener already understands. Familiarity matters more than cleverness. A comparison from their work or daily life is usually easier to inspect than an ornate metaphor.

sections.title: 3. Map the important relationship
sections.html: Say what corresponds to what. Keep only the relationship needed for the explanation, such as flow through a bottleneck, temporary storage or repeated practice.

sections.title: 4. State where the analogy stops
sections.html: Add a short boundary such as the comparison only describes the flow, not the underlying mechanism. This prevents a useful shortcut from becoming a false model.

sections.title: 5. Test the listener's paraphrase
sections.html: Ask the listener to restate the original idea rather than repeat the metaphor. If the wrong detail survives, revise the mapping or choose a different comparison.

editorialCuration.reason: Replace an inherited NLP-branded article containing invented comprehension, recall and laboratory statistics with a neutral communication practice that tests an analogy through listener paraphrase and explicit boundaries.
